clue.text: Using any sails in storm may result in breakdown

indicators.note: sails caught in a storm are thrown about, so the letters named before it get tossed into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters, exactly the answer's length

explanation.surface: A sailor hoisting canvas in a gale and wrecking the boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The nautical picture makes 'breakdown' read as a mechanical failure at sea; here it is the analytical sense, the answer ANALYSIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A breakdown of figures or a problem is a detailed examination of its parts, which is exactly what analysis means.

clue.text: You'll find this admiral in the hold

definitions.meaning: the British admiral who won at Trafalgar in 1805 and whose column stands in Trafalgar Square
a wrestling grip in which the arm is passed under the opponent's and the hand pressed on the neck

explanation.surface: An admiral found below decks, down in the ship's cargo hold.
explanation.walkthrough: The admiral makes 'hold' look like the cargo space of a ship; it is a wrestling hold, the half nelson or full nelson.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio Nelson is Britain's most famous naval commander, and a nelson is a named grappling grip used in wrestling.

clue.text: Nothing to do at this end

definitions.text: Nothing to do at this end

parts.note: the surface reads as idleness, someone with no task at hand
the setter's reading completes a stock phrase: the missing word slots in before 'end' to describe a person with nothing to do

explanation.walkthrough: To be 'at a loose end' is an idiom for having nothing to do; the clue gives the meaning and asks which kind of end.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'at a loose end' means idle and unoccupied, so this word is the one qualifying the end in that phrase.

clue.text: Drivers aren't slow to fall into it

definitions.text: Drivers aren't slow to fall into it

parts.words: aren't slow to fall into it
parts.note: the surface suggests drivers eagerly falling into some pit or habit
the setter's reading is literal: motorists who are not going slowly get caught by it

explanation.surface: Motorists who readily fall into some bad habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aren't slow to' is an idiom for 'are quick to', but read literally it means the drivers are speeding.
explanation.definitionFit: Police set up concealed camera or radar checks on roads, catching motorists who exceed the limit, a snare for fast cars.

clue.text: Snake dispatched, pierced by monarch softly

indicators.note: something pierced has a thing driven into it, so the word for dispatched takes the monarch and 'softly' inside

parts.note: dispatched a letter = sent it
Elizabeth Regina, the usual crossword monarch
piano, the musical direction to play softly

explanation.surface: A snake killed by a king's quiet thrust.
explanation.walkthrough: The monarch and 'softly' join up first and then go inside the word for dispatched, splitting it after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Serpent is a literary or biblical word for any snake, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Man — a Scottish isle? Could be!

parts.note: to man a post is to staff it
used as printed

explanation.surface: Someone wondering whether the Isle of Man counts as a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like the Isle of Man, which is not Scottish; it is the verb, to man. Staffa is a small Hebridean island famous for Fingal's Cave.
explanation.definitionFit: Staffa is an uninhabited island in the Inner Hebrides off Mull, known for its basalt columns and sea cave.

clue.text: Excursion for everyone within the bounds of Surrey

indicators.note: everyone is placed inside those two edge letters, as a crowd within a county border
a county's bounds are its edges, so only the first and last letters of Surrey are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of SurreY
everyone = all

explanation.surface: A day trip for the whole family in the Surrey countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is a county just south of London; only its two edge letters are used, with the word for everyone set between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a brief outing or trip, an old sense alongside a sudden charge out of a besieged fort.

clue.text: They run up volcano with long striding gaits

indicators.note: in a down clue, running up means reading from the bottom, so the volcano is written backwards

parts.note: Etna, the Sicilian volcano
a lope is a long easy running stride

explanation.surface: Hikers bounding up the side of a volcano with long strides.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' turns the volcano bottom to top. 'They run' is a thin definition, fair because the grazers are famous for running.
explanation.definitionFit: Antelopes are swift African and Asian grazing animals, known for fleeing predators at speed, so they are runners.

clue.text: Italian city girl

definitions.meaning: the Tuscan capital, Firenze in Italian
any female first name will do for 'girl'; this one was popularised by the nursing pioneer named after the city

explanation.walkthrough: 'Girl' in crosswords often means any female first name; here it happens to share a name with the city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Renaissance centre of Tuscany shares its English spelling with a female forename given in honour of it.

clue.text: Shady nook the French set back by bay

indicators.note: setting something back moves it backwards, so the French article is written in reverse

parts.note: la, the French feminine article
a small sheltered bay

explanation.surface: A secluded, shaded corner set back from a bay on the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set back' reads as a place lying away from the shore; it turns the French article round.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcove is a recess set into a wall or a sheltered garden bower, a small retreat out of the light.

clue.text: Great-aunt perhaps showing delight after run

indicators.note: the word for delight comes after the abbreviation for run, placing it second

parts.note: R = run, as on a cricket scoreboard
delight = elation

explanation.surface: An elderly great-aunt beaming with pleasure after a jog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' flags that a great-aunt is one example of the answer, not a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A great-aunt is one example of a relative, a family member connected by blood or marriage.

clue.text: Very lazy dizzy blonde, English, one's embraced

indicators.note: to be embraced is to be hugged within arms, so the numeral one goes inside the jumble
someone dizzy is spinning and confused, so the letters of blonde plus English are jumbled

parts.note: anagram fodder
E = English, added to the fodder
one = I, the Roman numeral; the 's is 'one is'

explanation.surface: A flaky English blonde being hugged, a lazy sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dizzy blonde' is a stock phrase, which hides 'dizzy' as the instruction; the numeral one then sits inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Bone-idle is an informal British intensifier meaning utterly lazy, idle to the very bones.

clue.text: Barked shrilly or deeply when disturbed

indicators.note: disturbing something knocks it out of place, so the letters of deeply are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A dog woken up, barking high or low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrilly or deeply' looks like a pair of alternatives about pitch; 'or' only joins the definition to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A yelp is a short sharp high cry, typically a dog's, so it is a bark pitched high.

clue.text: With hindsight, vet should keep on time or about

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the word for vet holds the short pieces inside

parts.note: to vet something is to inspect it
on = about = re, as in a memo heading
T = time

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so 'or' is written backwards

parts.note: used as printed

explanation.surface: Looking back, a vet ought to have stuck to the timetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like the memo word re, but that job falls to 'on'; 'about' turns 'or' round. The three short pieces go inside the word for vet after its IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking back on events with later knowledge is what the phrase means, an exact idiomatic synonym for hindsight.

clue.text: Idiot shows no end of charm after bottomless neglect

indicators.note: without a bottom means losing the last letter, the foot of the word for neglect
read literally rather than as 'plenty of', it strips the final letter from the word for charm
the shortened charm word is placed after the shortened neglect word

parts.note: neglect = ignore, losing its final letter
charm = amuse, losing its final letter

explanation.surface: A fool whose neglect leaves him quite without charm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of charm' reads as 'plenty of charm'; it means the word for charm with its end removed.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignoramus is an ignorant, uninformed person, close enough to a fool to serve as a crossword synonym.

clue.text: Tom in suffering sent out for soothing remedies

indicators.note: something suffering is in a bad state, so 'Tom in' and 'sent' are knocked into disorder
'out' here means out of order, backing up the instruction to rearrange the letters

parts.note: anagram fodder, first part
anagram fodder, second part

explanation.surface: Tom, in pain, is sent out to buy something to ease it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suffering' and 'sent out' fit the picture of a patient seeking relief, and both signal that the letters of 'Tom in' and 'sent' are scrambled.
explanation.definitionFit: Ointments are greasy salves rubbed on the skin to relieve pain or heal, which makes them calming treatments.

clue.text: Sunny spots?

parts.note: the surface reading suggests places that get plenty of sunshine, holiday destinations
the setter's reading: small marks on the skin brought out by the sun

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'spots' means blemishes, not locations.
explanation.definitionFit: These small brownish marks on fair skin darken and multiply with exposure to sunlight, so they are marks caused by the sun.

clue.text: They brought mother and father up well, presumably!

definitions.text: They brought mother and father up well, presumably!

parts.words: They brought mother and father up well
parts.note: the surface reading praises some people who raised a couple well
the setter's reading: the people who raised your mother and father, with 'well' hinting at the word grand

explanation.surface: Praise for the people who did a good job raising Mum and Dad.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue hints that the ones who raised your mother and father did it grandly, hence the name for them.
explanation.definitionFit: Your mother's and father's own parents are your nana and grandad, the older generation who reared them.

clue.text: Thoroughgoing cad and liar needing to reform

indicators.note: to re-form is to be formed again, so the letters of cad and liar are put into a new shape

parts.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A complete rotter and fibber who ought to mend his ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reform' fits the moral picture of a bad man improving, and is the instruction to rearrange the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Radical change goes to the root, meaning complete and far-reaching, the same sense as a thorough overhaul.

clue.text: Feel composer's final part is twisted

indicators.note: twisting turns a thing round, and 'final part' limits that to the last two letters of the composer

parts.note: George Frideric Handel, composer of Messiah; the 's is 'composer is'

explanation.surface: The ending of a composer's work takes a dark turn.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the last two letters of the composer's name are turned round, the start is left alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To handle something is to touch or finger it with the hands, the same as to feel it.

clue.text: Travel at speed and overheat

definitions.meaning: informal verb for driving or riding very fast along a road
to burn the surface of something with too much heat

explanation.surface: A car driven so hard that its engine runs too hot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as cause and effect, speeding making the engine hot; 'and' only joins two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To scorch is informally to race along, and also to singe or burn something by too much heat.

clue.text: That man arranged to go north, being excited

parts.note: he = that man

indicators.note: in a down clue north is upwards, so the word for arranged is read from the bottom

parts.note: to put things is to place or arrange them

explanation.surface: A man who got worked up after planning a trip up north.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, going north means reading upwards, so the word for arranged is written bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: Het up is an informal British phrase for agitated or worked up, from a dialect form of heated.

clue.text: Bad comedian is diabolical

indicators.note: something gone bad is spoiled and disordered, so the letters of comedian are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A critic's verdict on a comic who died on stage: truly dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad comedian is diabolical' reads as a review; 'bad' is the instruction, and 'diabolical' is the colloquial word for awful turned back into its literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Demoniac means like or possessed by a demon, and diabolical means of the devil, so both are fiendish.

clue.text: This person's gripped by organ sound

indicators.note: to be gripped is to be held, so the setter's pronoun sits held inside the body part

parts.note: the nose is an organ of the body
this person = I, the setter speaking; the 's is 'is', part of the container instruction

explanation.surface: Someone clinging to a church organ as it sounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' suggests music to go with 'sound'; it is the body part, and 'this person's' is the setter speaking of themself.
explanation.definitionFit: Noise is any sound, especially a loud or unwanted one, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Like the weather, boiling up but not cold inside

indicators.note: the phrase subtracts the word after it, and 'inside' says the loss comes from the middle

parts.note: a situation boiling up is building to its climax
C = cold, as on a tap, taken from the middle

explanation.surface: Weather that is heating up outside yet not cold within.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words differ by one letter: drop the C from the middle of the word for building to a peak.
explanation.definitionFit: Climatic means relating to climate, the long-term pattern of a region's weather conditions.

clue.text: Water nymphs in a sad novel

indicators.note: as an adjective novel means new, so the letters of 'in a sad' are made into a new word

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: Water nymphs appearing in a gloomy work of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' reads as a book, and is the adjective meaning new, so the three words before it are made anew.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek mythology naiads are the female spirits who live in rivers, springs and fountains.

clue.text: Goes through customs at university

parts.note: customs = usages, uses
a British student is 'up' at university, especially Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: A student returning from abroad passing through passport control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes through customs' reads as the airport check; the definition is 'Goes through' in the sense of consuming, and 'customs' is habits.
explanation.definitionFit: To go through supplies or money is to consume or exhaust them entirely, the same as depleting them.

clue.text: Declined to be escorted around German city

indicators.note: the word for escorted goes around the German city, holding it within

parts.note: escorted = led
Essen, the city in the Ruhr

explanation.surface: Someone who refused an escorted tour of a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Declined' looks like refused, to go with the escort; it is the sense of dropped or diminished.
explanation.definitionFit: Lessened means became smaller or reduced, the same as declined in the sense of fell away.
